title: Quantum Algorithms and Hardness for Point-Count Approximation over Finite Fields
abstract: We study the approximation of the number of solutions of Laurent polynomials over finite fields. For a Laurent polynomial \[f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{s}a_jx^{u_j}\in \mathbb{F}_q[x_1^{\pm1},\ldots,x_n^{\pm1}], \] let $U$ be its augmented support matrix whose columns are $(1,u_j)$ with rank $ρ$ and $N(f) := \# \{x\in (\mathbb{F}_q^\times)^n \mid f(x)=0\}$ be its torus point count. Our first main result is a quantum algorithm that outputs $\widehat{N}(f)$ satisfying \[ |\widehat{N}(f) - N(f)| \le \varepsilon q^{n+s/2-ρ} \] with success probability $1-δ$. Provided that $ρ$ and $\|U\|_\infty$ are bounded, the algorithm runs in both classical bit and quantum gate complexity $\mathrm{poly}(n, s, \log q, 1/\varepsilon, \log(1/δ))$. It provides finer resolution than relative-error approximations in general settings. To the best of our knowledge, in the explicit finite-field input model considered here, no previous algorithm achieves this additive accuracy with running time polynomial in $\log q$. Van Dam (arXiv:quant-ph/0405081) conjectured the existence of such an algorithm under the assumption of an oracle reflecting the algebraic properties of the polynomial. In contrast, by exploiting a point-counting formula derived from character sums over finite fields, we develop an alternative approach that efficiently approximates the number of points without assuming the existence of such an oracle. As a second main result, we prove that the same approximation problem becomes $\#$P-hard under randomized polynomial-time Turing reductions when the support matrix $U$ varies freely as part of the input. Thus, taken together, our results clarify how the effectiveness of the quantum approach depends on the tradeoff between the accuracy scale and the support parameters of the input polynomial.
summary: This paper develops a quantum algorithm to efficiently approximate the number of solutions to Laurent polynomials over finite fields, achieving an additive error bound. It also proves that the general version of this counting problem is $\#	ext{P}$-hard. The work clarifies the trade-off between the required accuracy and the structural complexity of the input polynomial.
main_problem: The paper addresses the problem of approximating the number of solutions, $N(f)$, to a Laurent polynomial $f(x)$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$.
main_result: It presents a quantum algorithm achieving an additive approximation guarantee for $N(f)$ under certain structural constraints on the polynomial's support matrix, and proves the problem is $\#	ext{P}$-hard when the support matrix varies freely.
method: The approach combines character sum expansions derived from algebraic geometry with quantum estimation techniques, specifically leveraging the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) for estimating Gauss sums.
model_or_system: The mathematical model is the set of solutions to a Laurent polynomial $f(x) = \sum a_j x^{u_j}$ defined over the multiplicative group $(\mathbb{F}_q^	imes)^n$. The complexity analysis is performed in terms of quantum gate and classical bit complexity.
key_observables: The primary observable is $N(f) = \#\{x \in (\mathbb{F}_q^	imes)^n \mid f(x) = 0\}$, and the algorithm estimates this value within an additive error bound $\varepsilon q^{n+s/2-ho}$.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the field size $q$, the polynomial support size $s$, the dimension $n$, and the rank $ho$ of the augmented support matrix $U$.
main_assumptions: The quantum algorithm's polynomial complexity relies on bounding the rank $ho$ and the infinity norm of the support matrix $\|U\|_{\infty}$. The hardness proof relies on the ability to recover the count from the approximation error.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the quantum algorithm for approximation (Theorem 1.2), followed by an alternative classical-quantum hybrid approach using character sums (Algorithm 1). It then establishes the computational hardness of the problem (Theorem 1.4 and Theorem D.3) by reducing from antichain counting.
why_interesting: While the problem is purely number-theoretic, the development of quantum algorithms to solve computationally hard counting problems over finite fields connects directly to quantum complexity theory and the limits of quantum computation.
